blocks.text: 我们所说的“智能体记忆”，是指 Claude 从经验中获得的知识——包括与用户的交互以及被指派的任务——并在会话之间保留下来，存为之后可以读取的上下文。它不包括模型学习或管理上下文的其他方式，例如改动权重（训练时设定的内部参数）、上下文学习（在单次对话中获得的知识），以及压缩（由 Claude 撰写的摘要，用来替换较早的对话轮次，以便它能在新的上下文窗口中继续工作）。

blocks.text: 记忆有时是一种预测。写下一条规则，就等于智能体在预测：它描述的这个模式以后还会派上用场。比如，记下一条已验证的事实，就是预测未来的会话中某个智能体会想直接依赖这条事实，而不必再核实一遍。随着时间推移，Claude 在这类预测上已经进步了很多。

blocks.text: 我们对比了 Claude Sonnet 3.7 和 Claude Fable 5 各一次运行中的记忆文件夹，当时两者都已进行到游戏约 10,000 步。我们注意到的一个关键差异，是每个模型认为什么值得记住。Sonnet 3.7 假定一切都可能有用，不加区分地写入记忆。它的记忆文件夹里存着各种遭遇的档案，往往为每一场战斗、每一件找到的物品、每一个遇到的非玩家角色各建一个文件。最终，Sonnet 3.7 在 225 个文件夹中写下了 413 个记忆文件，只拿到一枚徽章（徽章标志玩家在游戏中的进度）。

blocks.text: 我们还测试了给模型规定具体的记忆写入规则，每次测试只加一条规则。我们对比了每条规则下各模型从记忆中获得的提升，与没有规则时的提升。当我们把规则设为“只记录失败”时，Opus 5 和 Opus 4.7 从记忆中获得的性能提升都大幅缩水（图 5 右）。对更强的模型来说，让它们自行判断什么重要，比事先定死规则更有效，而那些规则反而可能削弱表现。

blocks.text: Claude 的 wiki 是逐步搭建起来的。在创建出初始 wiki 之后，它会利用后续几轮“做梦”来补充、编辑或删减内容。在“做梦”的早期轮次，Claude 的知识就像一个刚入职的新员工，仅凭 wiki 回答问题的能力有限。它“做梦”越多，知识地图就越丰富，就像一位经验丰富的老员工。在测试中我们发现，当我们同时给 Claude 提供搜索工具时，wiki 对它的帮助最大。当它同时使用搜索和 wiki 时，随着 wiki 不断扩充，其综合得分从 54% 升至 61%；而只提供搜索工具时，得分为 53%。如果只用 wiki 来回答问题，Claude 的最高得分为 48%。同时使用搜索和 wiki 还能为每个问题节省约 2 万个 token。

blocks.text: 如何为智能体设计记忆系统，还有许多未解的问题。其中之一是 Claude 应该在什么时候创建记忆。Claude 执行任务时，可以写入记忆存储（例如文件夹、文件或数据库），在源头捕捉重要信息，让关键细节能立即用于后续轮次或会话。但实时记录笔记难免会让 Claude 分心，偏离主任务。相比之下，做梦可以把记忆创建推到后台，但做梦的任何产出可能无法立即被 Claude 访问。

blocks.text: 另一个问题是如何让记忆可靠地保持最新。Claude 可能做出错误预测，或把一开始就错误的规则写入记忆。随着环境变化，记忆也可能漂移、变得无关。做梦是修正这些错误的一种方式（图 8），但需要消耗算力。让 Claude 持续检查所有记忆可能并不现实。更重要的也许是让做梦聚焦于可能变化的信息，或仔细调整做梦的节奏（例如根据记忆被访问的频率）。

blocks.text: As humans, we encode memory constantly as we go about our lives. The hippocampus plays a central role in this, capturing experiences in the moment so that memories form quickly and are immediately available. But only some experiences are consolidated into long-term knowledge.

blocks.text: Much of that consolidation appears to happen when our brains are offline. As we sleep, and during quiet rest, the hippocampus replays our recent experiences. This is thought to gradually distill those experiences and integrate them into the neocortex—the part of our brains that stores most of what we think of as knowledge.

blocks.text: Agent memory can use a similar division of labor. Agents capture much of their work in logs or transcripts. The same idea can help agents organize their memory by reflecting on logs to fix mistakes or produce new notes and representations. This process is often called dreaming (Figure 1).

blocks.text: By “agent memory,” we mean knowledge that Claude gains from experience—including interactions with users and tasks it’s been assigned—and that it retains between sessions, saved as context it can read later. blocks.text: Representations like wikis can help Claude traverse its ever-growing knowledge base. We explored the benefit of wikis as a memory representation using a corpus of internal documents—about 350,000 files, roughly 420M tokens—from Stainless, a software company we acquired in May. We created an evaluation set of 25 questions about this corpus and gave Claude a search tool to explore it. We also instructed Claude to build a wiki based on these files using dreaming. Over 128 sessions, we prompted Opus 5 agents to explore the files, write or correct linked wiki pages, merge duplicates, and check claims against the sources.

blocks.text: Claude builds its wikis incrementally. After creating an initial wiki, it uses subsequent rounds of dreaming to add to, edit, or prune it. In the early rounds of dreaming, Claude’s knowledge is like that of a new employee, and its ability to answer questions based on the wiki alone is limited. The more it dreams, the richer its knowledge map grows, like that of a seasoned employee. In our tests, we found that the wiki helped Claude the most when we also gave it access to a search tool. When it used both search and the wiki, Claude’s aggregate score rose from 54% to 61% as that wiki grew, compared with 53% when it had access to the search tool alone. Claude’s best score was 48% when it used only the wiki to answer questions. Using search and the wiki also saved about 20,000 tokens per question.

blocks.text: Promoting memories into a new session (a form of context injection) must be done carefully. Injected memories use up valuable tokens, and an incorrect note can be carried into every session. Loading a note also doesn’t guarantee that Claude acts on it: our documentation on Claude Code warns that longer instruction files reduce adherence. So the top layer of the memory hierarchy has to stay relatively small, and much of dreaming’s work here is keeping it that way—by moving some details down the hierarchy and leaving links behind.

inlines.text: Thinking backward, looking forward

blocks.text: There are many open questions about how to design memory systems for agents. One is when Claude should create memory. When Claude works on a task, it can write to a memory store (e.g., a folder, file, or database), capturing salience at the source and making important details immediately available for future turns or sessions. But logging notes in the moment inevitably draws Claude’s attention away from its main task. In contrast, dreaming can push memory creation to the background, but any outputs from dreaming may not be immediately accessible to Claude.

When Claude works on a task, it can write to a memory store (e.g., a folder, file, or database), capturing salience at the source and making important details immediately available for future turns or sessions. But logging notes in the moment inevitably draws Claude’s attention away from its main task. In contrast, dreaming can push memory creation to the background, but any outputs from dreaming may not be immediately accessible to Claude.

blocks.text: Another question is how to keep memory reliably up to date. Claude can make incorrect predictions or write rules to memory that are wrong from the start. Memory can also drift and become irrelevant as the environment changes. Dreaming is one way to fix these mistakes (Figure 8), but it requires compute. Directing Claude to continuously check all its memories might not be practical. It may be important instead to focus dreaming on information that’s likely to change or to carefully tune the cadence of dreaming (e.g., based on how often memories are accessed).

But Claude needs to use compute to maintain memory representations and make sure they don’t accumulate errors or hallucinations.

blocks.text: Even though Claude’s judgment about salience has improved, no model can really know what will happen in future turns. Dreaming gives Claude an opportunity to look backward and use compute to organize its memory, correct mistakes, and maintain representations that allow future sessions to access memory more readily. Memory systems will evolve as Claude gets more capable, and we still have a lot to learn about designing Claude’s memory systems.
